items.title: 2.3.2 Derivative of a Function Given in the Form of Parametric Equations

source_refs.note: Book p. 37-38: derivative of a function given by parametric equations x = f(t), y = g(t) via the chain rule; Example 4

blocks.text:
Let a function be represented by parametric equations
\[x = f(t) \quad \text{and} \quad y = g(t)\]
From \(x = f(t)\), we have
\[t = f^{-1}(x)\]
(Provided \(f\) is bijective)
Now, by Chain Rule applying to \(y = g(t)\) and \(t = f^{-1}(x)\), we get:
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy}{dt} \cdot \dfrac{dt}{dx}\]
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{\;\frac{dy}{dt}\;}{\frac{dx}{dt}}\]
\(\left(\because \frac{dt}{dx} = \frac{1}{dx/dt}\right)\)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What 'parametric' means: instead of one equation between \(x\) and \(y\), both are given in terms of a third variable \(t\), called the parameter. Think of \(t\) as time and \((x, y)\) as the position of a moving point: each value of \(t\) gives one point of the curve.
Why \(f\) must be bijective (one-one and onto): then each \(x\) comes from exactly one \(t\), so \(t = f^{-1}(x)\) exists and \(y\) really is a function of \(x\).
Why \(\frac{dt}{dx} = \frac{1}{dx/dt}\): the rate of \(t\) with respect to \(x\) is the reciprocal of the rate of \(x\) with respect to \(t\). This needs \(\frac{dx}{dt} \ne 0\).
Why this is useful: we never need to find \(f^{-1}\). We only differentiate \(x\) and \(y\) with respect to \(t\) and divide.

blocks.text_alt: dy by dx equals dy by dt divided by dx by dt, provided dx by dt is not zero

blocks.title: Example 4
blocks.problem: Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) if \(y = a\cos t\) and \(x = a\sin t\).
steps:
Given: \(y = a\cos t\), \(x = a\sin t\) (parametric equations with parameter \(t\)).
To find: \(\frac{dy}{dx}\).
Method: both \(x\) and \(y\) are given in terms of \(t\), so differentiate each with respect to \(t\) and divide: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\).

Step 1: Differentiate both equations w.r.t. t
\[\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -a\sin t\]
\[\dfrac{dx}{dt} = a\cos t\]
Why: \(a\) is a constant; \((\cos t)' = -\sin t\) and \((\sin t)' = \cos t\).

Step 2: Apply the Chain Rule
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\]
\[= -\dfrac{a\sin t}{a\cos t}\]
\[= -\tan t\]
Why: \(a\) cancels (\(a \ne 0\)) and \(\frac{\sin t}{\cos t} = \tan t\). We need \(\cos t \ne 0\).

Check: eliminate \(t\): \(x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}\sin^{2} t + a^{2}\cos^{2} t = a^{2}\), a circle. Differentiating \(x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}\) implicitly (2.3.3) gives \(2x + 2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0\), so
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x}{y} = -\dfrac{a\sin t}{a\cos t}\]
\[= -\tan t\]
Same answer.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our examples:
(a) \(x = t^{2}\), \(y = t^{3}\): \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 3t^{2}\), \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3t^{2}}{2t} = \frac{3t}{2}\) (\(t \ne 0\)).
(b) \(x = a\cos t\), \(y = b\sin t\) (an ellipse): \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{b\cos t}{-a\sin t} = -\frac{b}{a}\cot t\) (\(\sin t \ne 0\)).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Parametric form: \(x = f(t)\), \(y = g(t)\), with parameter \(t\).
2. \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\), provided \(\frac{dx}{dt} \ne 0\); it comes from the chain rule.
3. The answer is usually left in terms of \(t\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Dividing the wrong way: \(\frac{dx/dt}{dy/dt}\) gives \(\frac{dx}{dy}\), not \(\frac{dy}{dx}\).
2. Forgetting the minus sign of \((\cos t)' = -\sin t\).
3. Ignoring the points where \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 0\) (in Example 4, where \(\cos t = 0\)).
